claims.text: setState calls the given function synchronously, then marks the State's element dirty so build runs again (scheduled for the next frame).
claims.source_hint: Flutter API docs: State.setState ('The provided callback is immediately called synchronously… causes the framework to schedule a build')

claims.text: Changing a State field without setState does not cause a rebuild; the change shows only at the next build triggered by something else.
claims.source_hint: Flutter API docs: State.setState ('If you just change the state directly without calling setState, the framework might not schedule a build')

claims.text: setState rebuilds the calling State and updates the widgets below it; ancestors such as DonHangApp and MaterialApp are not rebuilt.
claims.source_hint: Flutter API docs: State.setState, State.build; refs/flutter-website ui/interactivity

claims.text: _reload is `setState(() => _products = widget.apiClient.fetchProducts())`, and the refresh FloatingActionButton's onPressed is _reload.
When FutureBuilder receives a new future, it goes back to waiting (showing the loading indicator) and builds again when the future completes.

LoginScreen._submit begins with one setState that sets _loading = true and _error = null, before awaiting the login request; the button then shows a CircularProgressIndicator and the error Text is removed.
Resizing the browser window causes the app to build again (MediaQuery change), so a changed field would then appear.
claims.source_hint: Flutter docs: MediaQuery-dependent widgets rebuild on size change (MaterialApp/Scaffold depend on MediaQuery)

claims.text: Rebuilding only the changed subtree keeps small changes cheap.
